Content:
Consider the following data set:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 100] | [MATH: 110] | [MATH: 120] | [MATH: 130] |
| [MATH: y] | [MATH: 12] | [MATH: 11] | [MATH: 12] | [MATH: 15] |

Content:
Our goal is to describe how to use matrices to carry out a linear regression. That is, we want to find an equation of the form

Content:
[MATH: y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x]

Content:
that best fits the given data points.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c0181831a6e790c04476f51670da497c]

Content:
Let's write our problem in matrix notation. Substituting the values of [MATH: x] into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of [MATH: y,] we obtain the system

Content:
[MATH: {β_{0} + 100β_{1} = 12; β_{0} + 110β_{1} = 11; β_{0} + 120β_{1} = 12; β_{0} + 130β_{1} = 15]

Content:
which can be expressed in matrix notation as

Content:
[MATH: [1|100; 1|110; 1|120; 1|130]]

Content:
The matrix [MATH: X] is called the design matrix, and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] is called the observation vector.

Content:
Since our points do not lie on a straight line, there will be no parameters [MATH: \beta_0] and [MATH: \beta_1] such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters [MATH: \beta_0] and [MATH: \beta_1] that best approximate the solution.

Content:
In other words, we seek to find a column vector [MATH: \boldsymbol\beta] such that

Content:
[MATH: \| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|]

Content:
is as small as possible.

Content:
Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.] Therefore, the coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem!

Content:
This approach to finding parameters for a linear regression model is often called ordinary least squares (OLS) regression.

Content:
Pre-multiplying the equation [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}] by [MATH: X^T,] we obtain the corresponding normal equation

Content:
[MATH: X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
Since the columns of [MATH: X] are linearly independent, the matrix [MATH: {X^T}X] is invertible, and

Content:
[MATH: {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: X] and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] into the formula above and simplifying, we get

Content:
[MATH: β^(^) = [1; 0.1].]

Content:
Therefore, the line of best fit (regression line) is

Content:
[MATH: y = 1+ 0.1x.]

Given a dataset of paired numerical observations [MATH: (x,y)] and the corresponding linear regression model [MATH: \widehat{y} =f(x),] the residual for a particular observation [MATH: (x, y)] is defined as

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/145cd294ca6ed57aab703f6fe2f0587e]

Content:
In the past, you may have seen that calculating a regression line typically means finding a line where the sum of the squared residuals
[MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^4 r_i^2]
is as small as possible.

Content:
Using matrix notation, the sum of the squared residuals can be viewed as

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^4 r_i^2 = \| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|^2.]

Content:
Therefore, the condition that the sum of the squared residuals is minimized is equivalent to minimizing [MATH: \| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|^2.] This, in turn, is equivalent to minimizing [MATH: \| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|.]

Content:
Therefore, the problem of minimizing the squared residuals is equivalent to solving the least squares problem for [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the following data set:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 100] | [MATH: 110] | [MATH: 120] | [MATH: 130] |
| [MATH: y] | [MATH: 12] | [MATH: 11] | [MATH: 12] | [MATH: 15] |

Content:
Our goal is to describe how to use matrices to carry out a linear regression. That is, we want to find an equation of the form

Content:
[MATH: y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x]

Content:
that best fits the given data points.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c0181831a6e790c04476f51670da497c]

Content:
Let's write our problem in matrix notation. Substituting the values of [MATH: x] into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of [MATH: y,] we obtain the system

Content:
[MATH: {β_{0} + 100β_{1} = 12; β_{0} + 110β_{1} = 11; β_{0} + 120β_{1} = 12; β_{0} + 130β_{1} = 15]

Content:
which can be expressed in matrix notation as

Content:
[MATH: [1|100; 1|110; 1|120; 1|130]]

Content:
The matrix [MATH: X] is called the design matrix, and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] is called the observation vector.

Content:
Since our points do not lie on a straight line, there will be no parameters [MATH: \beta_0] and [MATH: \beta_1] such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters [MATH: \beta_0] and [MATH: \beta_1] that best approximate the solution.

Content:
In other words, we seek to find a column vector [MATH: \boldsymbol\beta] such that

Content:
[MATH: \| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|]

Content:
is as small as possible.

Content:
Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.] Therefore, the coefficients of the line that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem!

Content:
This approach to finding parameters for a linear regression model is often called ordinary least squares (OLS) regression.

Content:
Pre-multiplying the equation [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}] by [MATH: X^T,] we obtain the corresponding normal equation

Content:
[MATH: X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
Since the columns of [MATH: X] are linearly independent, the matrix [MATH: {X^T}X] is invertible, and

Content:
[MATH: {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: X] and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] into the formula above and simplifying, we get

Content:
[MATH: β^(^) = [1; 0.1].]

Content:
Therefore, the line of best fit (regression line) is

Content:
[MATH: y = 1+ 0.1x.]

Content:
Given a dataset of paired numerical observations [MATH: (x,y)] and the corresponding linear regression model [MATH: \widehat{y} =f(x),] the residual for a particular observation [MATH: (x, y)] is defined as

Content:
[MATH: Residual|= Actual − Estimated; = y − f(x); = y − y^(^).]
We subtract the estimated value predicted by the model from the actual observed value. The residuals for the data set we considered earlier are shown below.

Content:
In the past, you may have seen that calculating a regression line typically means finding a line where the sum of the squared residuals
[MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^4 r_i^2]
is as small as possible.

Content:
Using matrix notation, the sum of the squared residuals can be viewed as

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^4 r_i^2 = \| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|^2.]

Content:
Therefore, the condition that the sum of the squared residuals is minimized is equivalent to minimizing [MATH: \| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|^2.] This, in turn, is equivalent to minimizing [MATH: \| \mathbf{y} - X\beta\|.]

Content:
Therefore, the problem of minimizing the squared residuals is equivalent to solving the least squares problem for [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.]
